rationales: One gram of water is 1/18 mole of molecules, and each molecule has three atoms, giving about 1.002 × 10²³ atoms.
This is approximately the number of water molecules in one gram, not the number of atoms.
This is about one-third of the correct atom count because it does not account for all three atoms in each molecule.
This is about twice the correct atom count and does not follow from the molar mass and three atoms per molecule.
CaP does not balance the charges of Ca²⁺ and P³⁻ ions.
CaP₂ does not balance the charges of Ca²⁺ and P³⁻ ions.
Ca₂P₃ has a net charge rather than the neutral ratio required for the compound.
Three Ca²⁺ ions and two P³⁻ ions balance to form neutral Ca₃P₂.
One gram contains vastly more than one atomic mass unit.
This is far fewer than the number of atomic mass units in one gram.
Since one atomic mass unit is about 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁴ g, one gram contains about 6.022 × 10²³ amu.
This is one-tenth of the correct number of atomic mass units in one gram.
C₂H₂ does not give the simplest whole-number ratio of carbon to hydrogen in C₆H₁₂.
CH has a 1:1 carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, unlike the 1:2 ratio in C₆H₁₂.
C₆H₁₂ is the molecular formula, not the simplest empirical formula.
Dividing the subscripts in C₆H₁₂ by six gives the empirical formula CH₂.
0.765 moles is too many for 25 g of a substance with a molar mass of about 98 g/mol.
0.51 moles is about twice the amount calculated from 25 g and the molar mass of H₂SO₄.
The amount is 25 g ÷ 98 g/mol, which is approximately 0.255 moles.
0.4 moles would require substantially more than 25 g of H₂SO₄.
6.02 × 10²³ atoms is the number of carbon atoms in one mole, or 12 g, of carbon.
12.04 × 10²³ atoms is twice the amount present in 6 g of carbon.
1.003 × 10²³ is too small because 6 g of carbon is half a mole, not one-sixth of a mole.
Six grams of carbon is 0.5 mole, containing about 3.01 × 10²³ atoms.
26 g is not the aluminum mass fraction of Al₂O₃ applied to 204 g.
27 g is not the aluminum mass fraction of Al₂O₃ applied to 204 g.
54 g is the aluminum content of one mole of Al₂O₃, which has a mass of about 102 g, not 204 g.
Aluminum makes up 54/102 of Al₂O₃ by mass, so 204 g contains 108 g of aluminum.
Urea has 28 g of nitrogen in about 60 g of compound, a smaller percentage than hydrazine.
N₂H₄ has 28 g of nitrogen in about 32 g of compound, giving the highest nitrogen mass percentage among these choices.
NH₃ has 14 g of nitrogen in about 17 g of compound, a lower percentage than N₂H₄.
NH₂OH has 14 g of nitrogen in about 33 g of compound, a lower percentage than N₂H₄.
One mole of carbon atoms can produce one mole of CO₂, which is less than ethane produces.
Diamond is elemental carbon, so one mole of its carbon atoms produces one mole of CO₂.
Each ethane molecule contains two carbon atoms, so one mole of ethane can produce two moles of CO₂.
Each methane molecule contains one carbon atom, so one mole of methane produces one mole of CO₂.
9.5 g is much more CaCO₃ than needed to react with the stated amount of HCl.
1.25 g is the mass of pure CaCO₃ needed, but the sample is only 95% CaCO₃.
The reaction requires 0.0125 mol CaCO₃, or 1.25 g pure CaCO₃; allowing for 95% purity gives about 1.32 g of sample.
1.45 g exceeds the amount required after correcting the pure CaCO₃ mass for 95% purity.
